questions.title: Section A — Question 1 (Case study: porphyria / CEP and CRISPR)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source describes porphyria — a group of genetic diseases affecting haem production — and Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria (CEP), a rare recessive form caused by a substitution mutation in the U1 gene on chromosome 10, which makes a faulty UROS enzyme (arginine replaces cysteine). Explain the meaning of the following terms:
1.1.1 Genetic counsellor
1.1.2 Chromosome
subQuestions.memoText:
1.1.1 (2 marks): a person who studies genetic conditions and family genetic history, and who supports, guides and gives options to people making decisions about inherited disorders (e.g. whether to have children).
1.1.2 (2 marks — any 2): a molecule / piece of DNA (genetic material) made of nucleotides; contains coding (genes) and non-coding DNA; wrapped around (histone) proteins; made of two chromatids joined at a centromere. (NOT simply "a strand of DNA".)

subQuestions.questionText:
For each term, decide which item(s) relate to it using: A — only item 1; B — only item 2; C — both; D — neither.
1.2.1 Term: Chromosome 10. Item 1: Autosome. Item 2: Sex-linked inheritance.
1.2.2 Term: CEP. Item 1: Polygenic. Item 2: Dominant gene.
1.2.3 Term: Protein synthesis. Item 1: tRNA. Item 2: mRNA.
1.2.4 Term: Mutated U1 gene. Item 1: Deletion mutation. Item 2: Substitution mutation.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.2.1 A (chromosome 10 is an autosome; the condition is not sex-linked)
1.2.2 D (CEP is caused by a single recessive gene — it is neither polygenic nor dominant)
1.2.3 C (both tRNA and mRNA are involved in protein synthesis)
1.2.4 B (the U1 mutation is a substitution, not a deletion)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Provide a word from the text that means the same as each statement:
1.3.1 Requires two of the same alleles to show the condition of CEP.
1.3.2 Process of making mRNA from DNA.
1.3.3 Change in nucleotide arrangement or sequence in DNA.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.3.1 Recessive / homozygous recessive
1.3.2 Transcription
1.3.3 Mutation (accept gene editing)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.5 is the pedigree of a family with CEP (A = normal allele, a = faulty allele; CEP is recessive). Parents 1 and 2 are unaffected but have an affected child (individual 3). Using 'A' and 'a':
1.4.1 Phenotype of female 1.
1.4.2 Genotype of individual 3.
1.4.3 Chance of parents 1 and 2 producing another child with CEP.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
1.4.1 Normal / unaffected (does not have the condition) (1).
1.4.2 Homozygous recessive — aa (1).
1.4.3 Both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa), so the chance is 25% (1/4 / 1 in 4) (2).

subQuestions.questionText: CEP occurs in about 1 in 74 300 individuals in South Africa. Use this to calculate the number of people out of 371 500 births expected to suffer from CEP. Show your working.

Give a scientific explanation, in terms of CEP, for each of the following 'vampire' characteristics:
1.6.1 Presence of fangs.
1.6.2 Drinking blood.
1.6.3 Emerge only at night.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.6.1 Withdrawal / recession of the gums, which makes the teeth appear longer (fang-like) (1).
1.6.2 Doctors once advised patients to drink animal blood as a source of haem / iron to treat the anaemia caused by CEP (1).
1.6.3 The skin is extremely sensitive to light and is damaged by sunlight, so sufferers avoid daylight and come out at night (1).

subQuestions.questionText: CEP is a serious disease, while 'vampires' have been portrayed as romantic or evil and powerful creatures in film and media. In your opinion, is this an offensive and unethical comparison? Give reasons for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 reasons, or 1–2 reasons explained (max 2 if no clear decision). NO — vampires are fictional, so no real person is harmed; the comparison educates the public about the condition; it helps explain historical beliefs about vampires and cultural history. YES — it makes light of a serious, life-threatening disease and shows disrespect; the 'evil' stigma of vampires could lead to sufferers of CEP being discriminated against, dehumanised or victimised; it undermines efforts to raise awareness of CEP as a genuine medical disease. (Mark the first stance only.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Figure 1.7 (CRISPR editing of the mutant U1 gene: the coding strand ATGGTTACCGCG is cut and repaired so that GCG becomes ACG) and Figure 1.8 (an mRNA codon table where GCN codons give arginine-region reading and the corrected codon gives cysteine; Cys = cysteine, Arg = arginine, Ser = serine).
1.8.1 From your own knowledge, provide ONE difference between DNA and RNA.
1.8.2 Provide the last two mRNA codons coded for by the corrected version of the U1 gene in step 4 of Figure 1.7.
1.8.3 The faulty U1 gene has been changed by swapping the nucleotide G with A (step 4). Refer to Figure 1.8 to explain how this change leads to the correct amino acid (cysteine) being present instead of arginine in the defective UROS enzyme.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.8.1 (2 marks — must compare the same feature in both): DNA is double-stranded, RNA is single-stranded; DNA contains deoxyribose, RNA contains ribose; DNA contains thymine (never uracil), RNA contains uracil (never thymine); DNA stores the genetic code, RNA carries it to the ribosome for translation; DNA is usually longer than RNA.
1.8.2 UGG UGC (2).
1.8.3 (3 marks): the corrected coding-strand triplet ACG is transcribed into the mRNA codon UGC (mark 'mRNA' once); UGC codes for cysteine (this mark only if 'cysteine' is linked to the correct codon); so a functional / normal UROS enzyme is made and haem synthesis proceeds, meaning the individual does not suffer from CEP.

questions.title: Section A — Question 2 (Case study: mtDNA, ancestry and DNA fingerprinting)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source describes mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA, ~16 500 base pairs, passed unchanged along the maternal line), the Y chromosome (passed unchanged from father to son), haplogroups, Prof Himla Soodyall's investigation into the ancestry of the Karretjie people, and a hospital baby mix-up resolved by DNA fingerprinting. Provide the correct biological term from the sources for each description:
2.1.1 A building block of nucleic acids, consisting of a pentose sugar joined to a nitrogenous base and a phosphate.
2.1.2 The process of swapping alleles between the chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
2.1.3 Cell division resulting in the halving of the ploidy / chromosome number.
2.1.4 Chromosomes of the same length with the same genes present at the same locus.
subQuestions.memoText:
2.1.1 Nucleotide
2.1.2 Crossing over
2.1.3 Meiosis (meiosis I)
2.1.4 Homologous (chromosomes)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Male gametes carry either an X or a Y chromosome. Refer to your knowledge of meiosis to explain how each gamete ends up with only one gonosome.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (4 marks): the X and Y chromosomes pair up (as a bivalent), lying opposite one another on the equator of the cell; during anaphase I of meiosis I, spindle fibres attached to the gonosomes contract and pull the homologous partners to opposite poles; so the X and the Y separate and end up in separate (haploid) daughter cells — each gamete therefore contains only one gonosome.

subQuestions.questionText: What is the chance of a son inheriting his father's Y chromosome? Explain your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: 100% (1). To be male a child must have a Y chromosome, and the only Y available comes from the father, so a father passes his Y chromosome to all of his sons (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the level of genetic variation in the nuclear DNA (nDNA) in a population is higher than that of mtDNA in a population.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (4 marks): there is far more nuclear DNA than mtDNA, so there is more scope for differences to arise through mutation; nDNA is a combination of DNA from two parents, while mtDNA comes from only one (the mother); nDNA undergoes crossing over, segregation and independent assortment during meiosis, producing unique new combinations of alleles; mtDNA does not undergo meiosis or crossing over, so it is simply a replicate of the existing mtDNA and stays much the same over generations.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to the sources on the investigation into the Karretjie people. Table 2.1 shows that 99% of Karretjie carry mtDNA haplogroup L0d (Khoisan), and Table 2.2 shows that 76,3% of Karretjie carry Y-chromosome haplogroup I (Caucasian). Explain how the results of the mtDNA and Y-chromosome haplogroup investigations support the maternal and paternal historical ancestry of the Karretjie people.
(Refer to Tables 2.1 and 2.2 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: 4 marks: mtDNA haplogroup L0d (the Khoisan haplogroup) is present in a very high proportion of Karretjie people (99% vs 76% of Khoisan), indicating that their maternal (female-line) ancestry is Khoisan; Y-chromosome haplogroup I (the Caucasian haplogroup) is present in a high proportion of Karretjie males (76,3%), indicating that their paternal (male-line) ancestry is European/Caucasian — matching the proposed history of Khoisan women having children with European farmers.

subQuestions.questionText: Are the results of an investigation like this important to the people of South Africa? Justify your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 reasons, or 1–2 explained (max 2 if no decision; mark the first stance only). YES: it verifies and adds to knowledge of the genetic history of an indigenous South African people; it can give the community a sense of identity and belonging; it shows how genetically similar different South Africans are, which can help counter discrimination; it documents the genetic effects of colonialism; it advances science. NO: it does not change or improve the living conditions of the Karretjie people; it is costly in time and money; it may reveal private or sensitive information about their history without full consent.

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Figure 2.6 (six gels showing DNA fingerprinting results for two sets of parents and two babies). What is a DNA fingerprint / profile?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): a pattern / picture of DNA bands that is unique to an individual; produced by cutting non-coding DNA into fragments and separating them by size using gel electrophoresis; used to identify a person or show relatedness (e.g. for paternity or crime-scene analysis) by comparing where the bands line up on the gel.

subQuestions.questionText: Why would non-coding DNA be used for the process of DNA fingerprinting / profiling?
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: coding DNA is very similar between all people, whereas non-coding DNA is far more variable — mutations in non-coding regions do not affect the individual, so these regions differ much more between people; this makes it easier to tell individuals apart and to produce a unique genetic profile.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use Figure 2.6 to determine the parents of baby 1 and baby 2. Justify your answers. The couples are Katjie & Hendrik and Plaatjie & Meitjies.
(Refer to Figure 2.6 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Baby 1 — Meitjies & Plaatjie (2). Baby 2 — Katjie & Hendrik (2). Justification: every DNA band in a baby's profile can be matched to a band in one or other of its two parents, because a child inherits half of its DNA from each parent; the bands in baby 1 match Meitjies and Plaatjie, and the bands in baby 2 match Katjie and Hendrik (so the babies were swapped).

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE other application of DNA fingerprinting / profiling.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: identifying suspects at a crime scene; identifying poached rhino horn or illegally traded organisms; authenticating food items (e.g. caviar, wine); identifying victims of disasters or soldiers killed in battle; tracing missing persons; diagnosing genetic disorders; matching tissue for organ transplants.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Sources A–E in the Source Material Booklet (the changing role of women in science; enrolment and academic-position statistics; society and the gender wage gap; a timeline of famous men and women in science; and awards, scholarships and recognition). Consider the statement:

"Women's contributions to genetic studies have received more credit over time."

Using the source material and your own knowledge, discuss your opinion in an essay of 2½–3 pages. You are expected to: read the sources carefully; take a definite stand; plan your essay before writing (the plan is marked and needs at least 3 facts, 1 counter-argument and 1 piece of own knowledge); present a debated argument using relevant information from Sources A–E plus your own Life Sciences knowledge; arrange the information to develop your argument; write in a scientifically appropriate way; and discuss at least nine different facts from the sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marked with the IEB essay rubric (40): Planning (6); Use of knowledge from sources (8) — 1–2 facts = 1, 3–5 = 2, 6–8 = 3, ≥9 = 4, plus integration; Use of own knowledge (4); Content relevance (2); Quality of argument supporting the decision (8); Fairness — counter-opinions integrated (4); Presentation (4); Scientific merit (4). Source credibility must be genuinely assessed, not a learned response. If a candidate merely lists names, cap at 2.

Examples of usable facts —
AGREE (more credit over time): female enrolment in the Wits genetics faculty in 2020 (2 569) is close to male (2 793) (B); the percentage of women in academic positions has risen markedly over the last 20 years (B); more women are now in prestigious roles (e.g. professor) and in laboratory work (B); McClintock won a Nobel Prize, Sakati has three genetic conditions named after her, and Doudna & Charpentier won the 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR — the first all-women team in the field (D); Israel proclaimed 2002 the year of advancing women in science and the UN declared 11 February the International Day of Women and Girls in Science (A); Mattel released Barbie dolls depicting women in genetics (E); the salary gender gap disappears among researchers in the highest positions (C); many female geneticists have received major awards and scholarships (E).
DISAGREE (still under-credited): women are still a small overall percentage in senior academic roles and in lab work (B); Yale/Yale-type studies show professors of both sexes rate an identical male CV more favourably and offer women lower salaries (C); Nettie Stevens, Martha Chase and Rosalind Franklin were overlooked while male colleagues received Nobel Prizes (D); Marie Maynard Daly (first Black American woman with a chemistry PhD, late 1940s) and Samia Temtamy (first Arab woman with a genetics doctorate, 1974) show how recently recognition came for non-Western women (D); few women win top research prizes even as the share of women professors rises (E); most scholarships for women in genetics are only offered in a handful of countries (E); most famous scientists named by the public are still men (A).
